intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the peripherin/RDS gene (PRPH2; also called RDS) on chromosome 6p. Homozygous mutation in PRPH2 has been found in patients with a severe early-onset form of the disorder. A digenic form of RP7 is caused by double heterozygosity for mutations in the PRPH2 and ROM1 genes.

paragraphs.text: Retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is a form of retinitis pigmentosa, a photoreceptor degeneration, caused by mutation in the gene that encodes peripherin/RDS, a photoreceptor-specific glycoprotein. It is usually inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with moderate severity, and its expression varies widely, even within families, where retinitis pigmentosa may occur alongside macular dystrophies (Kajiwara et al., 1991; Farrar et al., 1991; Weleber et al., 1993; Manes et al., 2015). Digenic inheritance has been described: only individuals heterozygous for mutations in both PRPH2 and ROM1 develop retinitis pigmentosa (Kajiwara et al., 1994). Homozygous PRPH2 mutations cause a severe early-onset retinal dystrophy with Leber congenital amaurosis or juvenile retinitis pigmentosa phenotypes (Wang et al., 2013).

paragraphs.text: Weleber et al. (1993) described 3 different phenotypes in 1 family that segregated a 3-bp deletion in the peripherin/RDS gene. The proband, a 75-year-old woman, presented at age 63 years with a profoundly abnormal electroretinogram (ERG) and adult-onset retinitis pigmentosa. Over 12 years the disease progressed dramatically, with marked loss of peripheral visual field. One daughter developed pattern macular dystrophy at age 31 years. At age 44 her ERG was moderately abnormal, but her clinical disease was limited to the macula. Another daughter presented with macular degeneration at age 42 years and over 10 years developed the clinical picture of fundus flavimaculatus. Her peripheral visual field was preserved, but her ERG was moderately abnormal. The son developed macular degeneration at age 44 years and had pericentral scotomas and a markedly abnormal ERG. Fluorescein angiography showed punctate pigment epithelial transmission defects.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2013) described 3 patients homozygous for PRPH2 mutations. Two had a clinical diagnosis of Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) and 1 had juvenile retinitis pigmentosa. All 3 had visual impairment within the first year of life, nondetectable or reduced ERGs, and a very similar maculopathy. The 2 patients with LCA also had nystagmus. In patient 1318, photographed at age 29 years, the fundus showed a prominent multilobulated central atrophic maculopathy surrounded by concentric rings of yellow deposits, with vessel narrowing and fine diffuse peripheral retinal changes. In patient 3256, photographed at age 66 years, the fundus showed peripheral and macular pigment deposits, choroidal sclerosis, vessel narrowing, optic disc pallor, and an extensive central atrophic maculopathy, and optical coherence tomography showed unusual globular lesions in the foveal region. In patient 741, examined at age 30 years, there was diffuse retinal dystrophy with retinal vessel narrowing, retinal pigment epithelium mottling and loss, and a multilobulated maculopathy. Visual acuity in this patient was 20/40. Family members heterozygous for these mutations were asymptomatic but had detectable maculopathy. The 56-year-old father of patient 741 had macular pattern dystrophy with clear-cut foveal changes and essentially normal visual acuity. At age 57 years, the mother of patient 1318 had 20/20 visual acuity, a florid butterfly-shaped macular pattern dystrophy, and retinal flecks. The 7-year-old son of patient 1318 showed a miniature form of foveal butterfly-shaped macular pattern dystrophy.

paragraphs.text: Manes et al. (2015) studied the clinical features of French patients with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa due to PRPH2 mutations. Disease severity was moderate: 78% of eyes had a visual acuity of 1 to 0.5, and 52% of eyes retained more than 50% of the visual field. Some patients had characteristic vitelliform deposits or macular involvement. In some families, some members had pericentral retinitis pigmentosa or macular dystrophy and others had widespread retinitis pigmentosa. Manes et al. (2015) concluded that PRPH2 mutations cause highly variable phenotypes and moderate forms of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa, including mild cases that might be underdiagnosed.

paragraphs.text: Using targeted next-generation sequencing, Wang et al. (2013) found a homozygous c.637T-C transition in the PRPH2 gene, resulting in a cys213-to-arg (C213R) substitution, in a patient with LCA (1318). The mutation had previously been associated with autosomal dominant pattern dystrophy. The patient's mother and son were heterozygous carriers. The 57-year-old mother was asymptomatic, with 20/20 visual acuity, but had a florid butterfly-shaped macular pattern dystrophy. The 7-year-old son had a miniature form of foveal butterfly-shaped pattern dystrophy. An unaffected brother was homozygous wildtype. The affected residue is conserved across species.
